blocks.text: Imagine a library system where each book must be uniquely identifiable, and every borrower must be linked to their borrowed books. How do we ensure data integrity in such a system?

blocks.markdown: In relational databases, keys play a crucial role in ensuring data integrity and establishing relationships between tables. This unit will explore candidate keys, primary keys, foreign keys, and integrity constraints, which are fundamental concepts in the relational model.

blocks.title: Candidate Key
blocks.text: A candidate key is a minimal set of attributes that can uniquely identify a tuple in a relation. A relation can have multiple candidate keys.

blocks.title: Primary Key
blocks.text: A primary key is a candidate key chosen by the database designer to uniquely identify tuples in a relation. It cannot contain NULL values.

blocks.title: Foreign Key
blocks.text: A foreign key is an attribute or set of attributes in one relation that references the primary key of another relation, establishing a link between the two tables.

blocks.title: Entity Integrity
blocks.text: Entity integrity ensures that every table has a primary key and that the primary key is unique and not NULL.

blocks.title: Referential Integrity
blocks.text: Referential integrity ensures that a foreign key value always points to an existing, valid tuple in the referenced relation.

blocks.title: Identifying Candidate and Primary Keys
blocks.prompt: Consider a relation `Students` with attributes (StudentID, Name, Email). Identify the candidate keys and choose a primary key.

steps.text: Identify attributes that can uniquely identify a student. Both StudentID and Email can uniquely identify a student, so they are candidate keys.
Choose one candidate key as the primary key. StudentID is typically used as the primary key because it is often a simple, numeric identifier.

blocks.answer: Candidate keys: StudentID, Email. Primary key: StudentID.

blocks.title: Understanding Foreign Keys and Referential Integrity
blocks.prompt: Consider two relations: `Orders` (OrderID, CustomerID, OrderDate) and `Customers` (CustomerID, Name, Email). Explain the role of the foreign key in maintaining referential integrity.

steps.text: Identify the foreign key in the `Orders` relation. CustomerID in `Orders` is a foreign key referencing CustomerID in `Customers`.
Explain referential integrity. The foreign key ensures that each CustomerID in `Orders` corresponds to a valid CustomerID in `Customers`, maintaining referential integrity.

blocks.answer: The foreign key CustomerID in `Orders` ensures that every order is associated with a valid customer in `Customers`, maintaining referential integrity.

blocks.title: Effect of Deleting Referenced Rows
blocks.text: Deleting a row that is referenced by a foreign key in another table can violate referential integrity. Database systems often provide options like cascading delete or restricting the delete operation.

points: Candidate keys are potential primary keys; a primary key is selected from them.
Foreign keys establish relationships between tables and ensure referential integrity.
Entity integrity requires primary keys to be unique and not NULL.
